steps.eyebrow: Practical Python type annotations for service interfaces
steps.title: Establish the rule

blocks.text: Describe the service function’s inputs and result. Distinguish accepting None from allowing the caller to omit an argument.
Use name: Type for a parameter and -> Type for the result. Hints alone do not validate runtime values.

Type | None admits None; = None separately allows omission. list[str] is a list of strings; set[str] a set of strings; tuple[int, str] a two-element integer/string tuple; dict[str, int] a string-to-integer dictionary.

annotations.text: Collection shapes describe element and key/value types.
The union allows None; the default separately allows omission.
The return hint describes the result, not runtime validation.

steps.eyebrow: Practical Python type annotations for service interfaces
steps.title: Why the distinction matters

blocks.text: Read shapes first, then defaults. Removing = None changes whether note can be omitted, not whether its type admits None. Removing | None changes admitted values, not defaults. An annotated interface still does not validate runtime values by itself.

steps.title: Reason through an example

blocks.text: For order_summary, item_names uses list[str], tags uses set[str], identifier_name uses tuple[int, str], and counts uses dict[str, int]. The return annotation describes the result. note: str | None still requires an argument; adding = None permits omission. These are interface descriptions, not runtime checks.
Adding a hint does not add runtime validation. Accepting None and allowing omission are different decisions.

public.prompt: Compare `def a(note: str | None):` and `def b(note: str | None = None):`. Which statement correctly describes omission and runtime validation?

options.text: Only b allows omission; both annotations permit None, and neither function’s hints alone enforce runtime validation.
Both allow omission, and their hints enforce runtime validation.
Neither allows omission, but b’s default enforces runtime validation.

option1.message: Correct: Only b allows omission; both annotations permit None, and neither function’s hints alone enforce runtime validation.

option2.message: Permitting None does not supply a default, and hints alone do not enforce runtime validation.

option3.message: b’s default permits omission; a default is not runtime validation.

steps.eyebrow: Python classes and instances for service models
steps.title: Establish the rule

blocks.text: Two order drafts need independent items, even though they share the class’s behavior.
A class statement creates a class with methods defining behavior. Calling that class creates an instance.

__init__(self, ...) initializes an instance; self.attribute stores its state. An instance method receives that instance first. Instance variables are specific to each instance; class variables are shared. For independent mutable values, create a fresh value on self inside __init__.

nodes.label: Alternative: one mutable class items shared by both

blocks.alt_text: Draft: shared method definitions → draft_a: self.items → fresh collection → draft_b: self.items → another fresh collection → Alternative: one mutable class items shared by both

steps.eyebrow: Python classes and instances for service models
steps.title: Why the distinction matters

blocks.text: Change only draft_a’s items and inspect draft_b. Calling Draft twice does not fix shared mutable class state. Assign a fresh collection to self during initialization. Shared methods use self to identify the instance being changed.

steps.eyebrow: Python classes and instances for service models
steps.title: Reason through an example

blocks.text: Draft defines behavior; draft_a and draft_b are instances. A fresh self.items in each __init__ gives each draft its own collection. One mutable items value on the class can instead be shared. Follow ownership: the method’s first argument identifies the instance, not a new copy of every attribute.
Two instances can still share a mutable class variable. Initialize fresh mutable state on self when independence is required.

To add the supplied item only to the first draft, write `draft_a.items.append(item)`. The list's `append(value)` method adds one value to that list. Because each initializer creates a fresh `self.items = []`, `draft_a.items` then contains the item while `draft_b.items` remains empty.

public.prompt:
Inspect this initialization:
```python
class Draft:
    def __init__(self):
        self.items = []
draft_a = Draft()
```
Which describes the class/instance relationship?

options.text: self is the shared class object rather than the method's instance.
Calling Draft creates an instance; __init__ stores items on that instance via self.
The class statement itself creates draft_a.

option1.message: An instance method receives the instance as its first argument.

option2.message: Correct: Calling Draft creates an instance; __init__ stores items on that instance via self.

option3.message: The class statement creates the class; calling that class creates the instance.

correct.message: Calling Draft creates an instance; __init__ stores items on that instance via self.

Type | None permits None, while a default such as = None separately permits omitting a Python function argument.
